Class 9 · Module 4 — Endocrine Panels

The Body's Messengers: Thyroid and Testosterone

Why hormones can only be read as feedback pairs, life-stage bands, and time-stamped snapshots — never as isolated numbers.

60 min read 8 cited sources

Two men, same lab, same week. Both get a testosterone result of 320 ng/dL, and both fall inside the reference range printed on the report. One is 68. For him, that number is unremarkable — squarely typical for his decade. The other is 26, and drew his blood at 4:30 in the afternoon after a poor night's sleep. For him, that same "in-range" 320 is a quiet alarm: it sits below where nearly all healthy men his age land on a morning draw, and the afternoon timing may have shaved 20% off the true morning value. Same number, opposite meaning.

This is the chapter where everything the course has been building toward converges. "In range is not optimal" has never been sharper than it is with hormones, because hormones are the markers where age, life stage, time of day, and feedback relationships all bear down on a single reported value at once. Read a hormone the way you'd read a cholesterol number — as a standalone figure judged against one universal cutoff — and you will misread it. This chapter teaches you to read the whole picture.

The decision frame, up front

Before the mechanisms, here is what you are actually trying to do when a thyroid or testosterone result lands in front of you. Everything after this section exists to make these judgments reliable.

For thyroid: never interpret TSH alone as if a bigger number were simply "more thyroid." TSH is the brain's demand signal, so it moves opposite to the hormone it regulates. Read it as one half of a pair with free T4 (and sometimes free T3). The pattern of the two together — not the position of either one in its range — tells the story.

For testosterone: a single number is close to meaningless until you know three things: the person's age, the time of day the blood was drawn, and whether you're looking at total or free testosterone. A "low" afternoon total in a young man may be a completely normal morning value in disguise; a "normal" total may hide a genuinely low free fraction when the binding protein is high.

Think About It

Before reading on: if TSH is a demand signal from the brain, would you expect it to rise or fall when the thyroid gland is underproducing hormone? Hold your answer — the thermostat analogy below will confirm it.

The thyroid axis as a thermostat

The single most useful mental model for the thyroid is a home heating system, and it is not a loose metaphor — clinicians use it deliberately (Andersen, 2025). Picture a thermostat on the wall and a furnace in the basement.

The pituitary gland in your brain is the thermostat. It senses how much thyroid hormone is circulating and decides whether the body is warm enough — metabolically speaking. The thyroid gland in your neck is the furnace: it produces the actual hormones, chiefly T4 (thyroxine, the storage form) and a smaller amount of T3 (the active form). The signal the thermostat sends to the furnace is TSH — thyroid-stimulating hormone.

Now the crucial move. When the room gets cold — when circulating thyroid hormone drops — what does a thermostat do? It calls for more heat. It turns the demand signal up. So when thyroid hormone is low, TSH goes up. When the room is too warm — thyroid hormone is abundant — the thermostat backs off, and TSH goes down. TSH and thyroid hormone move in opposite directions. This inverse relationship is the entire reason you cannot read TSH by itself and assume "higher is more thyroid activity." Higher TSH usually means the body is demanding more because it is getting less.

Why the pair beats either number alone

Consider four combinations of TSH and free T4, and notice how the pair resolves ambiguity that neither value could resolve alone:

High TSH, low free T4. The thermostat is screaming for heat and the furnace isn't delivering. This is the classic pattern of an underactive thyroid (overt hypothyroidism) — a clear prompt for medical evaluation.

High TSH, normal free T4. The thermostat is working harder than usual, but the furnace is (for now) keeping output in range. This "subclinical" pattern is exactly the situation where reading only free T4 would tell you nothing is wrong — and reading only TSH would leave you unsure how hard the system is straining. The pair reveals a system under load.

Low TSH, high free T4. The thermostat has shut off because the room is too hot — too much hormone. This overactive pattern (hyperthyroidism) again warrants evaluation.

Normal TSH, normal free T4. The reassuring case — but even here, "normal" hides a subtlety we'll return to.

Think About It

A friend proudly reports a "perfect" TSH but mentions they've felt sluggish and cold for months. What single additional number would most change how you read their result — and why would TSH alone be insufficient?

The relationship is a curve, not a straight line

Here is where the thermostat model earns an upgrade. The link between TSH and free T4 is not proportional — it is log-linear (Hoermann et al., 2015). A small drop in thyroid hormone produces a disproportionately large jump in TSH. The thermostat is exquisitely sensitive; it amplifies. This is precisely why TSH is such a good early-warning screen: it moves dramatically before free T4 has drifted far. But it is also why a TSH that looks "a little high" can correspond to a thyroid hormone level that has barely budged — the amplifier exaggerates the demand signal.

Hoermann and colleagues (2015) push the point further with two ideas worth carrying with you. First, each person has an individual set-point — the TSH–free T4 pairing that is normal for them sits in a much narrower band than the population reference range. Your personal "just right" thermostat setting might be a TSH of 1.0; someone else's might be 2.2. Both are inside the population range, but a shift from 1.0 to 2.2 could represent a real change for the first person even though every value stayed "normal." Second, the system contains multiple nested feedback loops, including a feedforward component — meaning "normal TSH" is a good screen but not a guarantee of optimal thyroid status.

This connects directly to a long-running debate about where the top of the "normal" TSH range should sit. Wartofsky and Dickey (2005) argued that the traditional upper limit of roughly 4.5 mIU/L was inflated because the reference populations used to define it were quietly contaminated with people who had undiagnosed thyroid disease. Strip those out, they contended, and 95% of genuinely healthy people have a TSH below 2.5 mIU/L. Whatever the final verdict — and the debate continues — the lesson for a careful reader is exactly the course's thesis: sitting inside the printed range is not the same as sitting where healthy people cluster.

The reference range tells you where the measured population landed. It does not tell you where you are healthiest — and for thyroid, the gap between those two ideas has been argued over for twenty years.

Testosterone: the number depends on what you measure

Switch systems. Testosterone introduces a complication thyroid doesn't have: most of it is not actually available to your tissues at any given moment. When you order a standard testosterone test, you usually get total testosterone — every molecule in the sample, whether it's free to act or not. But the vast majority is bound to carrier proteins in the blood, principally sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and, more loosely, albumin. Bound testosterone is like money locked in a fixed deposit — it's on your balance sheet, but you can't spend it. Only the small unbound portion, free testosterone, is immediately active.

This is why total and free can diverge, and why the divergence matters. SHBG is the governor. When SHBG rises — it climbs with age, with certain thyroid states, with some liver conditions — more testosterone gets locked up, so free testosterone can fall even while total stays normal. When SHBG drops — as it can with obesity, insulin resistance, or high insulin levels — total may read lower, yet a larger fraction is free. Read total alone in a person with unusual SHBG and you can be badly misled in either direction.

Practically: if a total testosterone result seems out of step with how a person presents, or if there's reason to suspect abnormal SHBG (older age, obesity, thyroid or liver issues), free testosterone — or at least an SHBG measurement to interpret the total — becomes essential rather than optional. The two numbers answer different questions. Total asks "how much is there?" Free asks "how much can act?"

Two confounders that change everything: time of day and age

Testosterone runs on a clock

Testosterone is not a steady level — in younger men it follows a pronounced diurnal rhythm, peaking in the early morning and drifting down through the day. The magnitude is large enough to flip a clinical interpretation. Travison, Araujo, and colleagues (2009) measured men across morning and afternoon clinic visits and found testosterone roughly 20–25% lower at 4 PM than at 8 AM in men aged 30–40. The single most instructive finding: among men who had at least one afternoon reading below the 300 ng/dL "deficiency" cutoff, seventeen had entirely normal levels on all three morning visits. The afternoon draw manufactured a diagnosis that the morning draw erased.

This is why reputable testosterone measurement is specified as a morning draw, ideally before 10 AM. A low afternoon result is not a finding — it's a scheduling artifact until confirmed in the morning.

Now a twist that ties the two confounders together. That daily rhythm is not fixed across the lifespan. Bremner and colleagues (1983), using 24-hour hourly sampling, showed that the characteristic morning peak is markedly blunted or absent in older men. This solved a historical puzzle: studies that sampled in the afternoon had failed to detect the age-related testosterone decline that morning-sample studies kept finding — because in young men the afternoon value is far below the morning peak, while in older men there's little peak to miss. In the Travison (2009) data, the morning-to-afternoon gap shrinks from ~20–25% at age 30–40 to only ~10% by age 70.

"Optimal" moves across the decades

This is the payoff of the age-banding thread the course has carried since Chapter 2, and the full treatment of the Chapter 1 warning about age-inappropriate testosterone. The universally quoted 300 ng/dL cutoff for "deficiency" was derived largely from studies of older men — and applying it to a young man is a category error. Zhu and colleagues (2022), analyzing NHANES data on roughly 1,500 men aged 20–44, derived age-specific middle-tertile ranges that are dramatically higher than the standard threshold: for men aged 20–24, the middle tertile ran 409–558 ng/dL. A 22-year-old at 320 ng/dL is technically "above the deficiency cutoff" yet sits below where the healthy middle of his age group lands. That is the exact scenario from this chapter's opening — the number is "in range" and simultaneously a sign that warrants a closer look.

Kelsey and colleagues (2014) added the modelling backbone. Their normative model, built from thirteen studies, shows total testosterone peaking around age 19 (~15.4 nmol/L), falling modestly to age 40, and then — strikingly — showing no further mean decline. What changes after 40 is the variance: the spread widens substantially, so the 95% prediction interval balloons from about 18.7 nmol/L at age 40 to 24.5 nmol/L at age 88. The practical translation: a single, age-independent reference range is indefensible. The same number means different things at different ages not only because the average shifts, but because the width of normal itself grows with age.

One more layer, because it complicates the tidy story. Travison and colleagues (2007), following the same men over time in the Massachusetts Male Aging Study, found a population-level testosterone decline beyond what aging alone explains — a within-person drop of roughly 1.6% per year against a cross-sectional age effect of only ~0.4% per year. In plain terms: successive generations of men appear to be running lower than age would predict, hinting at health, body-composition, and environmental cohort effects. So "normal for your age" is itself a moving target across time — another reason to read the individual trend, not just today's snapshot against a fixed line.

What lifestyle actually does — realistically

A candid word for anyone hoping to move these markers. Training, body composition, and sleep do influence hormones, but the honest magnitudes are more modest and more indirect than supplement marketing implies.

Sleep is the most direct lever for testosterone, because the morning peak is built during sleep. Chronic short sleep meaningfully depresses testosterone — this is well established, and it's the first thing to fix before concluding a value is "low." Body composition matters largely through SHBG and the metabolic milieu: excess adiposity and insulin resistance tend to lower SHBG and total testosterone, and losing fat mass can partially reverse this. Resistance training produces acute post-exercise hormone spikes, but these are transient and are not the driver of long-term muscle gain that older theories assumed; the durable benefit runs through improved body composition and insulin sensitivity, not through chronically elevated resting testosterone.

For thyroid, the lifestyle story is thinner: the axis is robust and self-correcting, and most meaningful thyroid abnormalities are not lifestyle-driven. Adequate iodine and selenium matter at the margins, and severe caloric restriction can transiently lower T3, but you cannot reliably "optimize" a healthy thyroid the way the internet suggests.

The governing principle throughout: these markers are worth understanding and tracking, but a clearly abnormal hormone result — a high-TSH/low-T4 pattern, a confirmed low morning testosterone in a young man, a suppressed TSH with high free T4 — is a prompt for medical evaluation, not a self-optimization project. The reader's job is to interpret intelligently and know when to escalate.

Worked example: putting the toolkit together

A 29-year-old reports fatigue. His panel: total testosterone 340 ng/dL, drawn at 3:45 PM; TSH 3.9 mIU/L; free T4 not ordered. Every value is "in range." Walk the toolkit.

Timing: a 3:45 PM draw at age 29 could understate the morning value by ~20–25% (Travison et al., 2009). The morning number might be near 420–450. Age band: even so, 340 sits below the middle-tertile floor for young men (~409 in the youngest band; Zhu et al., 2022) — worth a morning recheck rather than dismissal. Free vs total: without SHBG we can't tell if the free fraction is adequate; if SHBG is high, free could be lower than total suggests. Thyroid pair: a TSH of 3.9 is inside the traditional range but above the ~2.5 threshold Wartofsky and Dickey (2005) argued marks the healthy majority — and with no free T4, we can't distinguish a straining system from a comfortable one. Conclusion: not a diagnosis, but a clear case for a repeat morning testosterone, an SHBG or free testosterone, a free T4 to complete the thyroid pair, and — because fatigue plus these patterns is a real signal — medical evaluation. Notice that no single number triggered this; the combination, read through age, timing, and feedback, did.

Key Takeaways

  • Read thyroid as a pair: TSH is the brain's demand signal and moves opposite to thyroid hormone, so the TSH–free T4 pattern — not either number's position — carries the meaning.
  • The TSH–free T4 relationship is log-linear, and everyone has an individual set-point; "normal TSH" screens well but does not guarantee optimal thyroid status (Hoermann et al., 2015).
  • Total testosterone counts every molecule; free testosterone is what tissues can use. When SHBG is unusual, total and free diverge — measure SHBG or free when the total seems out of step.
  • Testosterone follows a diurnal rhythm: up to ~20–25% lower in the afternoon in younger men. A low afternoon value is a scheduling artifact until confirmed on a morning draw (Travison et al., 2009).
  • "Optimal" is age-banded: the 300 ng/dL cutoff came from older men; young men's healthy middle tertile is far higher (Zhu et al., 2022), and normal variance widens with age (Kelsey et al., 2014).
  • Sleep, body composition, and training move these markers modestly and indirectly — but a clearly abnormal hormone result is a sign that warrants medical evaluation, not a self-optimization target.
Looking Ahead

You've now seen how age, timing, and feedback reshape the meaning of a single number in the endocrine panels. In the next chapter we bring the whole course together: building a personal, longitudinal picture across every panel — reading your own trend line as the most powerful reference range you have, and turning "in range" into a set of decisions rather than a single reassuring word.
